message.content:
`docker start` is **not** the command to bring up the Docker daemon (the “engine”) – it’s used to start *containers* that were previously stopped. On Windows the Docker engine runs as a Windows Service called `com.docker.service`. To get Docker running you need to start that service (or launch Docker Desktop). Below are the ways you can do this: | Method | What it does | How to run | |--------|--------------|------------| | **PowerShell** | Starts the Docker service | ```powershell
Start-Service -Name com.docker.service
``` | | **Command Prompt** | Same as above but via `sc` | ```cmd
sc start com.docker.service
``` | | **Net command** | Classic way to start a service | ```cmd
net start com.docker.service
``` | | **Docker Desktop executable** | Launches the GUI app which will auto‑start the engine | ```cmd
"C:\Program Files\Docker\Docker\Docker Desktop.exe"
``` | | **Docker Machine** | If you’re using Docker Machine instead of Docker Desktop | ```cmd
docker-machine start default
``` | ### Quick test after starting Once the service is running, you can verify it with: ```bash docker version ``` If you see client and server information printed, Docker is up and ready. --- #### Why `docker start` won’t work `docker start ` expects a container name or ID. If you run it without an argument, Docker will complain: ``` Error: No such container: ``` So you can’t use it to start the Docker daemon itself. --- #### Common pitfalls 1. **Service already running** – If you try to start it again you’ll get “The service is already started.” 2. **Permission issues** – You may need to run PowerShell/Command Prompt as Administrator. 3. **Docker Desktop vs. Engine** – If you only have Docker Desktop installed, launching the `.exe` is enough; the underlying service will start automatically. Let me know if you’d like a one‑liner batch file that wraps all of this together!
